story.headline: Oil hit its highest since May on reports of planned US–Israeli strikes on Iran, while a tech-led stock sell-off pushed the US 10-year yield below 5%. The yen had its best day in a month.

reads.policy: Almost every major central bank is leaning toward raising rates because high oil keeps inflation up. A sharp fall in US bond yields today did not shake bets on a December Federal Reserve hike. Switzerland is the odd one out, where a cut is still possible.
reads.growth: The US jobs market is still strong, with layoffs near their lowest in decades. Elsewhere growth is softening at the edges: euro-area households are gloomier, UK factory orders fell and Canadian home prices slipped. None of it has changed central bank plans yet.
reads.inflation: Inflation is running hot almost everywhere because of energy, which is why so many central banks lean toward hikes. Canada's factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected, a sign more inflation is on the way there. Japan's inflation figures tonight matter most for the yen.
reads.risk: Investors turned nervous: tech shares fell sharply on doubts about AI spending, and reports of planned strikes on Iran added to the worry. Money went into US government bonds and the yen, while the New Zealand dollar fell most. Gold kept sliding instead of acting as a shelter.
reads.tot: Oil is at its highest since May on the risk of renewed strikes on Iran. That helps exporters like Canada and hurts big energy importers like Japan and the euro area.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds are betting most heavily against the Canadian dollar, even as a Bank of Canada hike looks likely, which leaves those bets exposed if the loonie keeps rising. They also bet against the kiwi and the euro. In the yen and the Aussie, hedge funds and long-term investors take opposite sides.
reads.fiscal: Government finances are weighing on the euro: France now pays more than 5% to borrow for ten years, and its gap over Germany is near the widest since 2011. Moody's reviews France's credit rating on Friday, and Britain's budget follows on October 28.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve is expected to hold rates on October 28 and raise them in December, because high oil is keeping US inflation up. That keeps US rates the highest among the big economies, though falling bond yields have taken some shine off the dollar.
fed.priced: October: hold expected; December: hike very likely.
fed.why: Energy-driven inflation is still too high for the Fed's comfort, and the jobs market is strong, with layoffs near their lowest in decades.
fed.watch: Friday's US business surveys and the University of Michigan's inflation expectations, then the decision on October 28. The Fed is in its quiet period until then.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada is expected to raise rates on October 28 after governor Tiff Macklem warned that energy will push inflation well above the bank's forecasts. Much of that is already in the Canadian dollar's price.
boc.why: High oil is lifting Canadian inflation, and factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected in September.
boc.watch: Canadian retail sales on Friday, then whether the bank signals more hikes after October 28; a hold would be the surprise.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand is expected to raise rates on October 28. Inflation cooled slightly in the third quarter but stayed above the bank's target, so the hike case held and supports the kiwi.
rbnz.priced: October 28: hike near certain; a second hike by February fully priced.
rbnz.why: Inflation is still above the bank's 1–3% target band, and core prices stayed firm even as the headline eased.
rbnz.watch: Whether the bank signals a run of hikes at its October 28 decision, or sounds content after one.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank is expected to hold on October 29 and lean toward a hike in December, as energy keeps euro-area inflation high. That supports the euro, but France's debt worries pull the other way.
ecb.priced: October 29: hold expected; December: hike likely.
ecb.why: Expensive energy is keeping euro-area inflation well above target, but gloomier households and France's rising borrowing costs argue for caution.
ecb.watch: Friday's business surveys and Moody's review of France, then what President Christine Lagarde says about December on October 29.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan is expected to hold on October 30, but a December hike is increasingly expected. The yen needs that hike, or clear signals of it, to recover from its weakness.
boj.priced: October 30: hold expected; December: hike likely.
boj.why: Inflation is close to the bank's 2% goal and it may raise its inflation forecast this month, which points toward a December move.
boj.watch: Japan's national inflation figures at 6:30 PM CT Thursday, and any hint from governor Kazuo Ueda about timing.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia may raise rates on November 3, with markets now seeing it as close to an even bet. Rising hike odds have lifted the Australian dollar to a three-week high.
rba.priced: November 3: hike close to even odds; December: hike more likely than not.
rba.why: Deputy governor Andrew Hauser said the inflation outlook has worsened, partly because of high oil, and some big banks now expect a November hike.
rba.watch: Australia's third-quarter inflation figures on October 28, the last big input before the November decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England is all but certain to raise rates on November 5 after UK inflation came in hotter than expected. The pound now moves on whether a second hike follows in December.
boe.priced: November 5: hike near certain; December: second hike a coin toss.
boe.why: Energy is pushing UK inflation far above the 2% target, and the jobs market is still strong.
boe.watch: UK consumer confidence tonight, retail sales on Friday and the October 28 budget, which may add help with energy bills.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds rates at zero and a December cut is still possible, because Swiss inflation is near zero. Its latest meeting summary showed it is comfortable with a weaker franc and no longer stands ready to intervene.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is barely above zero, and a strong franc keeps import prices low.
snb.watch: The bank's summary of its September policy discussion on Thursday, and any sign it is ready to cut or step into currency markets.

USD.summary: The dollar has the highest rates among the major currencies, with a Federal Reserve hike expected in December, but a rush into US bonds has pulled yields down and left it near a three-week low.

notes.policy: The Fed is expected to hold in October and hike in December, and a strong jobs market gives it no reason to back off.
notes.inflation: High oil keeps US inflation well above the Fed's goal, which supports the case for more hikes.

EUR.summary: The euro is held back by expensive energy and France's rising borrowing costs, and the European Central Bank is moving more slowly than the US and UK central banks.

notes.policy: The European Central Bank is expected to hold in October and is behind the Fed and the Bank of England in raising rates, which gives the euro less support.
notes.growth: The euro-area economy looks weaker than the US, with households gloomier and France's political strain weighing on it.
notes.inflation: Energy keeps euro-area inflation well above target, which pushes the central bank toward a hike.
notes.tot: Europe imports most of its energy, so high oil and gas prices drain money out of the region.
notes.fiscal: France now pays more than 5% to borrow for ten years, ahead of a credit rating review by Moody's.

GBP.summary: The pound is near its strongest against the euro in 17 months, because a Bank of England hike in November is all but certain after hot UK inflation.

notes.policy: A Bank of England hike on November 5 is nearly fully priced, with a second in December a coin toss.
notes.growth: UK jobs figures have stayed strong, giving the Bank room to raise rates, though factory orders are weak.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is running far above the 2% target, driven by energy.

JPY.summary: The yen is still weak because Japan's rates are far below everyone else's, but it just had its best day in a month as war and stock-market fears sent investors to safety.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rates are far below other major banks', though a December hike is increasingly expected.
notes.risk: The yen is a safe place to park money, so it gains when stock markets fall on war fears.
notes.tot: Japan imports most of its energy, so high oil drains money out of the country and weighs on the yen.

CHF.summary: The franc is held between two forces: it gains when fear rises, but near-zero Swiss inflation keeps the central bank leaning toward a cut.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is near zero, so the central bank has no reason to raise rates and may cut.
notes.risk: The franc is a safe place to park money, so it tends to gain when the Gulf conflict flares.

AUD.summary: The Australian dollar is near a three-week high on rising bets of a Reserve Bank of Australia hike in November, though it lags the safe havens when investors get nervous.

notes.policy: Markets see close to even odds of a Reserve Bank of Australia hike on November 3.
notes.growth: Australian jobs fell and unemployment rose to a five-year high, which tempers the case for hikes.
notes.tot: Firm prices for Australia's exports bring money into the country and support the currency.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar is supported by oil at its highest since May and a Bank of Canada hike expected on October 28, which hot factory prices have made look more justified.

notes.policy: A Bank of Canada hike on October 28 is close to fully priced.
notes.growth: Canada's housing and shopping figures have been soft, which could limit how far the bank goes after October.
notes.inflation: Factory and raw material prices jumped far more than expected, a sign more inflation is coming.
notes.tot: High oil lifts Canada's export income, which supports the currency.

NZD.summary: The kiwi is supported by a Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 that markets see as near certain, but it falls hardest when war and tech fears hit stock markets.

notes.policy: A Reserve Bank of New Zealand hike on October 28 is close to fully priced, with more expected by February.
notes.growth: New Zealand's factories are having their best stretch since 2021, giving the central bank room to raise rates.
notes.risk: Steady demand from China and a softer US dollar have helped the kiwi this month, though it still drops when stocks fall.
notes.tot: Firm dairy prices, New Zealand's biggest export, bring money into the country.
